Aim and objectives

Aim. To calculate absolute treatment effects and appraise a trial report for validity, including n-of-1 and cluster randomised designs.

At the end of this workbook, you should be able to:

  1. Calculate ARR, RRR and NNT (or NNH) from a trial's 2×2 table and interpret a NNT of 7.
  2. Convert between probability and odds and explain when the odds ratio approximates the relative risk.
  3. Explain why absolute measures are more useful than relative measures for clinical decisions.
  4. Describe n-of-1 and cluster randomised trials, including the design effect and intracluster correlation.
  5. Appraise a trial report for internal and external validity using randomisation, concealment, blinding, follow-up and generalisability.
  6. Complete all 30 worked challenges, scoring at least 24 (80%), before you open the working.
  7. Turn all 50 flashcards and mark at least 40 as 'Got it' by the end of today's session.

Part 1 · Core ideas

Category 113.11 · Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials

13.3.1.9Absolute risk reduction, number needed to treat and number needed to harm

Big idea. The number needed to treat turns a difference in risk into people: how many must receive the treatment for one more good outcome, over a stated time.
Picture it as how many lottery tickets you buy for one win.

Syllabus: Number needed to treat and number needed to harm (with absolute risk reduction, 13.3.1.11)

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 15 · Absolute and relative risk →

The story in plain words. If one ticket in ten wins, you expect to buy ten tickets for one prize. The number needed to treat works the same way. Take the difference in event rates, the absolute risk reduction ARR = CER minus EER, and turn it upside down: NNT = 1 / ARR. In the figure, 25 of 100 relapse on usual care and 15 of 100 on the new treatment. ARR is 0.10, so NNT is 10; RRR is 40%, which sounds far more dramatic. When the treatment causes an unwanted event, the same arithmetic gives the number needed to harm: absolute risk increase, then NNH = 1 / ARI. A trial with an adverse event in 8% on placebo and an NNH of 25 implies a 12% rate on the drug, because 1 / 25 = 4% is added to the placebo rate. Always convert counts to proportions first when arms differ in size, always round the NNT up, and always quote the time frame. ((? Nine of 300 relapse on drug, 12 of 200 on placebo. NNT over two years? ?)) CER 6%, EER 3%, ARR 3%; 1 / 0.03 = 33.3, so 34 over two years.

Icon array of 100 people per arm: absolute and relative risk reduction and the number needed to treat. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Cook and Sackett (1995) popularised the NNT as the clinically useful measure, and Altman (1998) showed how to put a confidence interval around it by inverting the limits of the ARR. Straus and colleagues teach adjusting the NNT to your own patient: divide by f, the patient's risk relative to the trial controls.

From everyday life to the clinic. Relative risk reduction is fairly stable across populations, but ARR depends on baseline risk. With a constant RRR of 30%, a baseline relapse risk of 10% gives ARR 3% and NNT 34 (33.3 rounded up); double the baseline risk to 20% and ARR becomes 6%, so NNT roughly halves to 17. High-risk patients gain most. That is why the NNT is the best single measure to discuss with a patient choosing between treatments: it speaks in people, not percentages. It still needs pairing with the NNH for important side effects and with the time frame.

One winner in ten cards: the number needed to treat. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Traps: using the relative rather than the absolute reduction for NNT, forgetting to convert counts when arms differ in size, rounding down, and assuming NNT is fixed across populations. An ARR of 0 means no difference between arms, not that nobody had the event. The size of an absolute difference is the same whichever way you subtract; its direction tells you benefit or harm.

Three NNT traps and their corrections. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Coronary Drug Project Research Group (1980). Influence of adherence to treatment and response of cholesterol on mortality in the Coronary Drug Project. New England Journal of Medicine, 303: 1038-1041.
  2. Lind J (1753). A Treatise of the Scurvy. Edinburgh: Sands, Murray and Cochran.
  3. Altman DG, Bland JM (1995). Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. BMJ, 311: 485.
  4. Sun X, Briel M, Walter SD, Guyatt GH (2010). Is a subgroup effect believable? Updating criteria to evaluate the credibility of subgroup analyses. BMJ, 340: c117.

13.3.1.13Appraising a trial report

Big idea. A trial is judged on its question, its methods and the honest reading of its interval: subgroups, surrogates, early stops and negative results all need sceptical handling.
Picture it as a referee reviewing match footage before trusting the scoreline.

Syllabus: Critically appraise controlled and uncontrolled trials

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 35 · Appraising a therapy paper →

The story in plain words. A scoreline means little until you check the footage: was the offside real, was the pitch level? Appraisal does the same for a trial. Start with the confidence interval and read it against two lines, as the figure shows: the line of no effect and the smallest clinically important difference. A trial whose interval sits wholly above the important line has shown benefit that matters; one wholly between the lines has shown a real but trivial effect; one that excludes an important benefit is truly negative; one that straddles both is simply inconclusive. A negative trial with p = 0.20 is not proof of no effect. If the end of its interval that favours treatment still includes a worthwhile benefit, the treatment may yet be useful. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. Power is the chance of detecting a true effect. It rises with more patients, a larger true effect, less variability, better adherence and a more lenient alpha. ((? Does tightening alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 raise power? ?)) No. A stricter threshold lowers power unless the sample grows.

Four trial results read against the line of no effect and the smallest important benefit. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Sun and colleagues (2010) listed criteria for a believable subgroup effect: specified in advance with its direction, one of few hypotheses, large and unlikely by chance, consistent across studies. Fleming and DeMets (1996) showed how surrogate end points such as lipid levels or HbA1c can mislead. Montori and colleagues (2005) warned that composite end points are valid only when components matter similarly to patients and move together. Bassler and colleagues (2010) showed that trials stopped early for benefit overestimate effects, most when few events have accrued.

From everyday life to the clinic. A ward activity programme reduced aggression at weeks 4 and 8, then the difference vanished after it stopped. That points to benefit while the programme runs, not failure. But scores also fell on usual-care wards, which raises the possibility of non-specific effects such as staff attention. Readmission, relapse, function and death are outcomes patients feel. Scores on memory tests or impulsivity scales used to stand in for them are surrogates.

A pilot's checklist for appraising a trial. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Subgroup questions reward the option about pre-specification. Composite end point questions reward the option about patients valuing components unequally as the reason NOT to use one. Early stopping questions: the commonest reason is an apparently large early benefit, and such trials overestimate. Power questions: the odd one out is the stricter alpha.

Test twelve subgroups and one will often look significant by chance. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Sources
  1. Altman DG, Bland JM (1999). How to randomise. BMJ, 319: 703-704.
  2. Killip S, Mahfoud Z, Pearce K (2004). What is an intracluster correlation coefficient? Crucial concepts for primary care researchers. Annals of Family Medicine, 2: 204-208.
  3. Zwarenstein M, Treweek S, Gagnier JJ, et al. (2008). Improving the reporting of pragmatic trials: an extension of the CONSORT statement. BMJ, 337: a2390.
  4. Greenhalgh T (2019). How to Read a Paper: The Basics of Evidence-Based Medicine and Healthcare, 6th ed. Wiley-Blackwell.
  5. Pablos-Mendez A, Barr RG, Shea S (1998). Run-in periods in randomized trials: implications for the application of results in clinical practice. JAMA, 279: 222-225.
  6. Braunholtz DA, Edwards SJL, Lilford RJ (2001). Are randomized clinical trials good for us (in the short term)? Evidence for a 'trial effect'. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 54: 217-224.

13.3.2The n-of-1 trial

Big idea. An n-of-1 trial randomises treatment periods within one patient, so the question becomes whether this treatment works for this person.
Picture it as taste-testing two coffees blind on alternate mornings.

Syllabus: n of 1 trial

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 104 · Crossover, cluster and factorial trials →

The story in plain words. If you want to know whether you truly prefer a new coffee, a friend can make it or your usual brand on random mornings without telling you which. After several pairs, the pattern speaks for you, not for coffee drinkers in general. An n-of-1 trial does this with treatment: pairs of periods on active drug and placebo (or two doses, or two drugs), the order randomised within each pair, patient and clinician blind, outcomes rated daily. The figure shows three such pairs. Scores sit near 3 on active periods and 6 on placebo, and the first days of each period are discarded as a washout so carry-over does not blur the comparison. ((? Why randomise the order within each pair? ?)) So that time trends and expectation cannot line up with the treatment.

Daily symptom scores across three randomised pairs of active and placebo periods in one patient. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

The people and the evidence. Guyatt, Sackett and colleagues (1986) at McMaster described n-of-1 trials in routine practice and found they often changed management, sometimes stopping a drug both patient and doctor had believed in. Senn's work on crossover designs supplies the statistics, since an n-of-1 trial is a multiple crossover in one person.

From everyday life to the clinic. The ideal setting: a chronic, stable condition; a treatment with rapid onset and offset; trials showing average benefit but many non-responders; and genuine uncertainty for this patient. Uses include doubt about whether a started drug helps, finding the best dose, testing whether a symptom is a side effect, and persuading a patient who insists on a treatment the clinician thinks is useless. Poor settings: acute or rapidly changing illness, self-limiting conditions, prevention of rare events such as stroke, irreversible or curative treatments, and drugs with long carry-over.

Blind coffee tasting in randomised pairs: an n-of-1 trial. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Questions ask when an n-of-1 trial is most suitable: choose the stable chronic condition with trial evidence of average benefit but uncertain individual response. When asked when it is not recommended, choose the treatment expected to cure permanently, or the acute, rapidly evolving illness.

When an n-of-1 trial fits and when it does not. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Hollis S, Campbell F (1999). What is meant by intention to treat analysis? Survey of published randomised controlled trials. BMJ, 319: 670-674.
  2. Spruance SL, Reid JE, Grace M, Samore M (2004). Hazard ratio in clinical trials. Antimicrobial Agents and Chemotherapy, 48: 2787-2792.

13.3.6.5Cluster randomised trials

Big idea. When groups such as wards or practices are randomised, people within a group resemble each other, so each extra patient adds less information and the trial must be larger.
Picture it as asking ten people from the same family their opinion.

Syllabus: Cluster randomised trials

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 106 · Crossover, cluster and factorial trials →

The story in plain words. Ask ten strangers about a film and you hear ten views; ask ten members of one family and you may hear one view ten times. Patients on the same ward share staff, routines and atmosphere, so their outcomes are correlated. A cluster randomised trial randomises the ward, practice or school, not the individual, usually because the intervention works at that level (a ward programme, a practice guideline) or because individual randomisation would contaminate the control arm. The intracluster correlation coefficient (ICC) is the share of total outcome variance that lies between clusters: between / (between + within). The design effect is 1 + (m minus 1) x ICC, where m is the average cluster size. In the figure, ten patients per ward with an ICC of 0.05 give a design effect of 1.45, so 400 patients carry the information of about 276 independent ones. ((? Does cluster randomisation increase or decrease power for the same number of patients? ?)) Decrease. The sample must be inflated by the design effect.

Design effect against average cluster size for three intracluster correlations. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Donner and Klar set out the design and analysis of cluster trials, and Killip and colleagues (2004) explained the ICC for clinicians. The CONSORT extension for cluster trials (Campbell and colleagues, 2012) asks reports to give the ICC, cluster numbers and sizes, and a flow diagram at both cluster and individual level.

From everyday life to the clinic. A trial randomising 40 wards to a structured activity programme or usual care used ANCOVA adjusted for baseline aggression. Group differences were significant at weeks 4 and 8 but not at week 12, after the programme stopped. Average scores say nothing about whether every patient improved. An ICC near 1 means the ward behaves like a single patient; an ICC of 0 means clustering costs nothing. The ICC usually comes from pilot data or earlier studies.

Ten strangers or ten relatives: why clustering reduces information. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. The ICC question asks what variability it describes: between clusters (wards), not within a ward and not between arms. Power questions: cluster randomisation reduces effective sample size. Results questions: read the p values at each time point and do not infer that every individual responded.

What the intracluster correlation coefficient measures. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.
Sources
  1. Laupacis A, Sackett DL, Roberts RS (1988). An assessment of clinically useful measures of the consequences of treatment. New England Journal of Medicine, 318: 1728-1733.
  2. Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.
  3. Fleming TR, DeMets DL (1996). Surrogate end points in clinical trials: are we being misled? Annals of Internal Medicine, 125: 605-613.

13.3.7Internal and external validity of trials

Big idea. Internal validity asks whether the result is true for the people studied; external validity asks whether it holds for your patients. Size cures random error, never bias.
Picture it as a dartboard: grouping is precision, hitting the bull is validity.

Syllabus: Internal and external validity of trials

Read more in your textbookResearch Methods, page 110 · Trial phases and validity →

The story in plain words. On a dartboard, a tight group of darts in the top corner is precise but wrong; darts scattered evenly round the bull are right on average but imprecise. The figure shows the four combinations. Bias is a systematic shift away from the truth and threatens internal validity. Random error is scatter, and it shrinks as studies grow. A huge biased trial simply lands its darts ever more tightly in the wrong place. Internal validity is protected by randomisation, concealment, blinding, complete follow-up and intention-to-treat analysis. External validity, or generalisability, depends on who was recruited, the setting, the intervention as delivered and the outcomes chosen. ((? Do small studies suffer more from random error or from bias? ?)) Random error; bias does not shrink with size.

Bias and random error shown as darts on a target. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

The people and the evidence. Campbell and Stanley (1963) named the threats to validity in before-and-after designs, including testing effects: sitting the same test twice raises scores without any learning. Braunholtz and colleagues (2001) reviewed the trial effect, the tendency for control patients in trials to do better than similar patients outside them, through selection of less ill patients, closer monitoring, protocol-driven care and expectation. Rothwell (2005) set out the questions a clinician should ask before applying a trial to the patient in front of them.

From everyday life to the clinic. A ward team sits a knowledge test, has teaching, then sits the identical test again and scores rise. With no control group, a practice effect explains much of the gain. Trial participants are often younger, less comorbid and more adherent than clinic patients, especially after a run-in. The result can be internally valid and still not transfer.

Trial room versus clinic: internal and external validity. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Where the exam tries to catch you. Random error versus bias: random error dominates small studies and affects reliability; bias affects validity and does not disappear with size. For the trial effect, the factor that does NOT explain it is randomisation itself, which balances arms within the trial but does not make trial patients better than outsiders.

A bigger biased trial: narrower interval, same wrong place. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
Sources
  1. Campbell MK, Piaggio G, Elbourne DR, Altman DG (2012). Consort 2010 statement: extension to cluster randomised trials. BMJ, 345: e5661.
  2. Guyatt G, Sackett D, Taylor DW, et al. (1986). Determining optimal therapy: randomized trials in individual patients. New England Journal of Medicine, 314: 889-892.
  3. Campbell DT, Stanley JC (1963). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research. Rand McNally.
  4. Schulz KF, Altman DG, Moher D, for the CONSORT Group (2010). CONSORT 2010 Statement: updated guidelines for reporting parallel group randomised trials. BMJ, 340: c332.

Category 213.4 · Measures of treatment impact

3.2.12.1Odds, probability and the odds ratio

Big idea. Probability compares the people affected with everybody; odds compare them with the people who were spared, and that single difference is why the two numbers diverge as an outcome becomes common.
Picture it as a bookmaker counting the room.

Syllabus: Odds, probability and the odds ratio

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 25 · Odds ratios versus relative risks →

The story in plain words. A clinician counts the room one way and a bookmaker counts it another. Of 25 patients, 10 are psychotic. The clinician says the probability is 10/25, because probability is those with the outcome over everybody. The bookmaker says the odds are 10/15, because odds are those with it against those without. The two convert easily: odds are p divided by 1 minus p, and probability is odds divided by 1 plus odds. At low probabilities they are nearly the same number, which is why the distinction can be ignored for rare events. At 90% the odds are 9 to 1, and the two have parted company entirely. The odds ratio is the odds of the outcome in the exposed divided by the odds in the unexposed, which from the 2 x 2 table is ad / bc. Its null value is 1, and below 1 means lower odds in the first group. ((? Why does a case-control study report an odds ratio and never a relative risk? ?)) Because the investigators fixed how many cases there were, so no risk can be calculated from the design.

Probability (risk)Odds
Definitionwith / allwith / without
Ten psychotic among 25 patients10 / 25 = 0.4010 / 15 = 0.67
Convertingodds = p / (1 minus p)p = odds / (1 + odds)
When the outcome is rare (p below 10%)0.050.053: odds and risk almost equal
When the outcome is common0.804.0: odds far exceed risk
Twenty-five patients, ten psychotic: the same facts give a probability of 0.40 and odds of 0.67. Odds ratios exaggerate relative risks when outcomes are common

The people and the evidence. Bland and Altman (2000) wrote the BMJ note that the exam leans on. Their central warning is that the odds ratio approximates the relative risk only when the outcome is rare, under about 10%. With a common outcome the odds ratio sits further from 1 than the relative risk and therefore overstates the effect. The odds ratio survives in spite of that because of where it comes from. Case-control designs can produce nothing else, and logistic regression, the standard way of adjusting for confounders with a binary outcome, outputs adjusted odds ratios.

From everyday life to the clinic. Take relapse at 40% on placebo and 20% on drug. The relative risk is 0.5. The odds ratio is 40/160 divided by 80/120, which is 0.375, noticeably further from 1. Both describe the same trial. If a paper reports an odds ratio for an outcome that happened to 40% of the control group and discusses it as though it were a risk, the effect has been quietly inflated, and a reader who does not know the difference will pass that inflation on to a patient.

Probability compares the red people with everyone (10 of 25 = 0.40). Odds compare the red people with the grey people (10 to 15 = 0.67). Same crowd, two fractions

Where the exam tries to catch you. The commonest trap is treating OR and RR as interchangeable. Check the control event rate: if it is above about 10%, they are not. The second is the direction of the 2 x 2. Compute ad / bc with the table the wrong way round and you get the reciprocal, which is the odds ratio for the comparison you did not want. The third is the null value: 1 for any ratio, 0 for any difference.

Sources
  1. Bland JM, Altman DG (2000). The odds ratio. BMJ, 320: 1468.

3.2.12.2Absolute and relative measures

Big idea. A relative figure tells you how much the risk shrank; an absolute figure tells you how much risk there was to shrink, and only the second one tells a patient what to expect.
Picture it as half off, on two very different price tags.

Syllabus: Relative risk, absolute and relative risk reduction, absolute and relative benefit increase

Read more in your textbookEvidence-Based Medicine, page 14 · Absolute and relative risk →

The story in plain words. Half off a thousand pounds and half off a pound are both fifty per cent. That is the whole lesson. The control event rate is the proportion with the outcome in the control arm, the experimental event rate the proportion in the treated arm. Relative risk is EER divided by CER, with a null of 1. Absolute risk reduction is CER minus EER, with a null of 0. Relative risk reduction is the ARR divided by the CER, which is the same as 1 minus the relative risk. For a good outcome the identical arithmetic is renamed absolute benefit increase and relative benefit increase. Work it through. Relapse 40% on placebo and 20% on drug: RR 0.5, ARR 20%, RRR 50%. Response 60% against 45%: ABI 15%, RBI 33%.

A 50% relative risk reduction, twice. High baseline: ARR 20 points, NNT 5. Low baseline: ARR 2 points, NNT 50. The relative figure is the same; the absolute benefit is ten times smaller

The people and the evidence. Cook and Sackett (1995) made the argument that changed how trials are reported. Relative measures travel between populations because they are ratios, which is exactly why they are quoted in advertising: they sound the same size everywhere. Absolute measures depend on the baseline risk, and that dependence is the information a patient needs. The relationship is simply ARR equals RRR times CER.

From everyday life to the clinic. Put numbers on it. A 50% relative risk reduction gives an ARR of 20% when the control risk is 40%, and an ARR of 1% when the control risk is 2%. Same headline, twenty times the difference in what the patient gets. So the question to ask of any impressive relative figure is what the baseline risk was. ((? A drug halves the risk of a complication. What do you need before you can advise? ?)) The control event rate, because without it the halving could be worth a great deal or almost nothing.

Relative risk 0.5 (half as many relapses); relative risk reduction 50%; absolute risk reduction 20 people in every 100. The relative figure sounds bigger, the absolute figure is what the ward will notice

Where the exam tries to catch you. The stem that reports only a relative risk reduction and asks what you would tell the patient is asking for the absolute figure, and usually the number needed to treat with it. The second trap is the null values, which differ: 1 for the relative risk, 0 for the absolute reduction. The third is direction. For a good outcome the same arithmetic is a benefit increase, and a stem may switch from relapse to response mid-paragraph.

Sources
  1. Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat. BMJ, 310: 452-454.
  2. Bland M (2015). An Introduction to Medical Statistics, 4th ed. Oxford University Press.

Challenge 1 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.9
ArmRelapse, nNo relapse, nTotal, n
New drug12288300
Placebo15235250
Total27523550
Relapse over two years in a maintenance trial. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In a two-year maintenance trial, 12 of 300 patients on a new drug relapse, compared with 15 of 250 on placebo. Using the table, how many patients need to take the new drug for two years to prevent one relapse?
  1. 2
  2. 20
  3. 60
  4. 50
  5. 500
Show the working
Answer: D 50

The arms differ in size, so convert counts to proportions first: EER = 12 / 300 = 0.04; CER = 15 / 250 = 0.06.

ARR = 0.06 minus 0.04 = 0.02 and NNT = 1 / 0.02 = 50. Give the time frame: 50 patients treated for two years prevent one relapse.

Rule: NNT = 1 / ARR, with ARR = CER minus EER from proportions, not raw counts.
Trap: Subtracting raw counts (15 minus 12) instead of rates.
Rates before differences when arms differ in size. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Challenge 2 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.1.9
ArmWeight gain over 7%, nNo weight gain over 7%, nTotal, n
Olanzapine alone80120200
Olanzapine plus metformin50150200
Total130270400
Weight gain at six months in adults starting olanzapine. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
In patients starting olanzapine, the 6-month risk of gaining more than 7% body weight is 40%. Co-prescribed metformin lowers this to 25%. Using the table, how many patients need metformin to prevent one such weight gain?
  1. 3
  2. 7
  3. 15
  4. 25
  5. 40
Show the working
Answer: B 7

ARR = 40% minus 25% = 15%. NNT = 100 / 15 = 6.7.

Always round the NNT up, because you cannot treat part of a patient and rounding down overstates the benefit: 7 patients over six months.

Rule: NNT = 100 / ARR(%), rounded up to the next whole patient.
Trap: Taking the ARR percentage as the NNT.
Rounding the NNT up. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Challenge 3 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.6.5
Mean ward aggression score (higher is worse)Week 0Week 4Week 8Week 12
Activity programme: 20 wards, 210 patients58.250.146.354.0
Usual care: 20 wards, 190 patients57.954.655.256.1
Adjusted p (ANCOVA for baseline)baseline0.030.0020.31
Cluster randomised trial of a ward activity programme; the programme ran from week 0 to week 8. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A cluster RCT randomised 40 adult acute inpatient wards in 12 trusts: 20 wards (210 patients) delivered an 8-week ward-wide structured activity programme and 20 wards (190 patients) continued usual care. The sample size was inflated for the expected intracluster correlation and dropout. The primary outcome was a validated ward aggression score (higher is worse), measured at weeks 0, 4, 8 and 12; the programme stopped at week 8. Between-group differences were tested by ANCOVA adjusting for baseline score. What kind of randomisation was used?
  1. Simple individual randomisation
  2. Cluster randomisation
  3. Stratified quota allocation
  4. Minimisation
  5. Multistage random sampling
Show the working
Answer: B Cluster randomisation

Whole wards were allocated, so every patient on a ward received the same condition: cluster randomisation.

It suits ward-level interventions and avoids contamination between patients, but patients within a ward resemble each other.

Rule: Allocating groups (wards, practices, schools) = cluster randomisation.
Trap: Thinking each patient was individually randomised.
Cluster allocation: whole wards are randomised. Teaching illustration, The Complete Doctor Academy.

Source: Campbell MK, Piaggio G, Elbourne DR, Altman DG (2012). Consort 2010 statement: extension to cluster randomised trials. BMJ, 345: e5661.

Challenge 4 · 13.11 Appraising therapy: randomised and other trials · 13.3.7
Mean team score on the identical 30-item test before and one week after the teaching session. Illustrative data drawn for CDA.
A ward team sits a 30-item knowledge test on rapid tranquillisation, attends a half-day teaching session, and one week later sits the identical test again. The whole team takes part, not a low-scoring subgroup. Mean scores rise from 58% to 74% (figure). Apart from a genuine teaching effect, which explanation best accounts for the rise?
  1. Recall bias
  2. Confounding by indication
  3. Practice effect from sitting the same test twice
  4. Lead-time bias
  5. Publication bias
Show the working
Answer: C Practice effect from sitting the same test twice

Sitting the identical test twice raises scores by familiarity and recall alone: the testing or practice effect, a threat to internal validity in any uncontrolled before-and-after design.

Only a comparison group that sits the same two tests without the teaching can show how much of the 16-point gain belongs to the course. Parallel forms of the test also help.

Recall bias, confounding by indication, lead-time bias and publication bias each belong to other settings.

Rule: Repeating an identical measure inflates scores: the testing (practice) effect.
Trap: Crediting the course for gains that a control group sitting the test twice would also show.
Testing effect: only the difference in gains belongs to the teaching (control team illustrative). Illustrative data drawn for CDA.

Source: Campbell DT, Stanley JC (1963). Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Research. Rand McNally.

Show the working
Answer: B 10/15

Probability divides by the whole group; odds divide by those without the event. Ten psychotic patients against fifteen non-psychotic gives odds of 10 to 15, or 2 to 3.

Rule: Odds = with / without. Probability = with / all.
Trap: Giving 10/25, which is the probability.
Odds divide by the other group: 10 to 15 (2 to 3); probability divides by everyone: 10 of 25 = 0.4

Source: Bland JM, Altman DG (2000). The odds ratio. BMJ, 320: 1468.

Challenge 6 · 13.4 Measures of treatment impact · 3.2.12.1
Outcome at 28 days for 100 patients admitted under section
The figure shows the outcome at 28 days for 100 patients admitted under section: the probability of discharge within 28 days is 0.80. What are the odds of discharge within 28 days?
  1. 0.20
  2. 0.25
  3. 0.80
  4. 1.25
  5. 4
Show the working
Answer: E 4

Probability is the chance of an event out of all possibilities, a number between 0 and 1. Odds compare the chance of the event with the chance of the non-event, and run from 0 to infinity. A probability of 0.5 is odds of 1 (evens); a probability of 0.8 is odds of 4 (4 to 1 on).

Odds = 0.80 / (1 minus 0.80) = 0.80 / 0.20 = 4. To convert back, probability = 4 / (1 + 4) = 0.8.

The exam offers the complementary probability and the inverted odds as distractors; write out p / (1 minus p) every time.

Rule: Odds = p / (1 minus p); probability = odds / (1 + odds).
Trap: Inverting the fraction and giving the odds against.
Probability 8 out of 10 = 0.8; odds 8 against 2 = 4

Source: Altman DG (1991). Practical Statistics for Medical Research. Chapman & Hall.

Challenge 7 · 13.4 Measures of treatment impact · 3.2.12.1
Event during one yearProbability
Verbally abused by a patient0.3
Involved in a serious incident0.2
Annual probabilities of two independent events in a cohort of junior doctors
The table shows, for a cohort of junior doctors, the probability of being verbally abused by a patient during a year and the probability of being involved in a serious incident. The two events are independent. What is the probability that a doctor is neither verbally abused nor involved in a serious incident during the year?
  1. 0.06
  2. 0.44
  3. 0.50
  4. 0.56
  5. 0.80
Show the working
Answer: D 0.56

Two events are independent when one happening tells you nothing about the other. The probability that both occur is then the product of their probabilities, and the same multiplication rule applies to the complements: the probability that neither occurs is the product of the two 'not' probabilities.

P(not abused) = 1 minus 0.3 = 0.7. P(no incident) = 1 minus 0.2 = 0.8. P(neither) = 0.7 x 0.8 = 0.56. For contrast, P(at least one) = 1 minus 0.56 = 0.44, and P(both) = 0.06.

The exam's favourite wrong answer is the subtraction 1 minus 0.3 minus 0.2 = 0.5, which would only be right if the events could never occur together.

Rule: For independent events, P(neither) = (1 minus p1) x (1 minus p2).
Trap: Adding probabilities as if the events were mutually exclusive.
Independent events: 0.3 x 0.2 = 6 have both, so 30 minus 6 and 20 minus 6 have one only, leaving 56 with neither

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Oxford: Blackwell.

A national primary care database (covering about 4% of the population) was used to identify 9,860 adults with bipolar disorder admitted with serious self-harm, each matched to two controls with bipolar disorder who were not admitted. The table shows the univariable results. Which factor is the strongest predictor of admission?
  1. Alcohol dependence
  2. Previous admission for self-harm
  3. Benzodiazepine prescription
  4. Lithium prescription
  5. Living alone
Show the working
Answer: B Previous admission for self-harm

An odds ratio compares the odds of exposure among cases with the odds among controls. Values above 1 indicate the exposure is more common in cases, values below 1 that it is less common. Strength is judged by the distance from 1 on the log scale, so OR 4 and OR 0.25 are equally strong, and significance by whether the confidence interval excludes 1.

Reading down the table, previous self-harm admission at OR 4.1 (3.2 to 5.3) dwarfs every other factor. Lithium at 0.6 is the equivalent of OR 1.67 in the other direction, still weaker than 4.1.

Tables like this are built to tempt you with the most clinically interesting row; the arithmetic answer is the row with the largest OR whose CI excludes 1.

Rule: The strongest association is the odds ratio furthest from 1 (on the log scale), provided its interval excludes 1.
Trap: Picking a factor that is clinically salient rather than the one with the largest odds ratio.

A national case-control analysis compared the method of suicide in people with a diagnosis of autism with that in age- and sex-matched people without autism. The odds ratios are shown. What was the commonest method of suicide in the group with autism?

  2. Overdose
  3. Hanging
  4. Drowning
  5. Cannot be determined from this information
Show the working
Answer: E Cannot be determined from this information

An odds ratio for a method of suicide compares the odds of that method in cases with the odds in controls. A value of 1.9 means the method is relatively more frequent in cases, but a method that accounts for 2% of deaths in controls and 4% in cases would produce a similar OR, while a method accounting for 50% in both groups would produce an OR of 1. Without the underlying counts, ranking by frequency is impossible.

The table lists only ORs and intervals. Nothing in it gives the proportion of autistic people dying by each method, so the question has no answer from these data.

'Cannot be determined' is a legitimate and sometimes correct option; the exam uses it when a stem supplies relative measures and asks an absolute question.

Rule: Ratio measures compare groups; they never tell you absolute frequency.
Trap: Reading the largest odds ratio as the most frequent category.
MethodShare of suicides, controlsShare of suicides, casesOdds ratio
A rare method2%4%about 2
A common method50%50%1
An odds ratio of about 2 can belong to a method used in 4% of deaths while the commonest method, used in half of all deaths in both groups, scores an OR of 1; ratios alone cannot rank frequency

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Oxford: Blackwell.

Autoimmune thyroid disease in a case-control study of bipolar disorder
A case-control study examines whether a history of autoimmune thyroid disease is associated with bipolar disorder. The table shows the results: among 1000 cases with bipolar disorder, 8 have autoimmune thyroid disease; among 1000 controls, 2 do. The odds ratio for exposure in this study is approximately
  1. 0
  2. 2
  3. 4
  4. 6
  5. -4
Show the working
Answer: C 4

A case-control study starts from disease status and looks back at exposure, so you cannot calculate risks. You can calculate the odds of exposure in cases and in controls and compare them. Arrange the data as cases exposed (a), cases unexposed (b), controls exposed (c) and controls unexposed (d); the odds ratio is the cross-product (a x d)/(b x c).

Here a = 8, b = 992, c = 2, d = 998. OR = (8 x 998)/(2 x 992) = 7984/1984 = 4.02, which rounds to 4. When the exposure is rare, as it is here, the odds ratio is close to the simple ratio of exposed counts (8/2 = 4) because b and d are nearly equal to the group totals.

The negative option is a reminder that odds and their ratios are always zero or positive; a negative value can only be a sign that someone has subtracted when they should have divided.

Rule: Odds ratio = (a x d)/(b x c) from the 2x2 table; it is never negative.
Trap: Subtracting counts instead of forming the cross-product ratio.
StepWorkingResult
1Lay out the table: a = 8, b = 992, c = 2, d = 998Cases exposed, cases unexposed, controls exposed, controls unexposed
2Cross-product (a x d)/(b x c) = (8 x 998)/(2 x 992)7984/1984
3Divide4.02, rounds to 4
ShortcutExposure rare, so b and d are nearly 10008/2 = 4
The cross-product gives 4.02; because the exposure is rare, the simple ratio of exposed counts gives the same 4.

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Current smoking in 120 patients and 120 accompanying relatives
The table shows smoking in 120 consecutive patients attending an alcohol service, of whom 90 are current smokers, and in 120 non-dependent relatives who accompany patients to the same service, of whom 45 are current smokers. By what factor are the odds of smoking greater for a patient than for a relative?
  1. 0.2
  2. 0.6
  3. 2
  4. 3
  5. 5
Show the working
Answer: E 5

Odds compare those with a characteristic to those without it in the same group. Among the patients, 90 smoke and 30 do not, so the odds of smoking are 90/30 = 3. Among the relatives, 45 smoke and 75 do not, so the odds are 45/75 = 0.6. The odds ratio is 3/0.6 = 5.

The cross-product gives the same answer without working out each odds separately: (90 x 75)/(30 x 45) = 6750/1350 = 5. The ratio of proportions (0.75/0.375 = 2) is a different measure; because smoking is common in both groups, the odds ratio is much larger than the risk ratio.

Draw the table every time. Questions give you only the exposed counts and expect you to fill in the unexposed cells yourself.

Rule: Build the 2x2 table, then OR = (a x d)/(b x c).
Trap: Dividing the two proportions instead of the two odds.
Odds of smoking are 90 to 30 (3.0) among patients and 45 to 75 (0.6) among relatives: 3.0/0.6 = 5, while the ratio of proportions (75% versus 37.5%) is only 2.

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Start by completing the table. Cases: 30 exposed, 120 unexposed. Controls: 12 exposed, 138 unexposed. The odds of exposure in cases are 30/120 and in controls 12/138. Dividing one odds by the other and rearranging gives the cross-product (30 x 138)/(12 x 120).

Numerically that is 4140/1440 = 2.9, so people with agoraphobia had nearly three times the odds of childhood residence near a major road. The point of this question is the structure, not the number: pair each group's exposed count with the other group's unexposed count.

The option with 150s in it is the ratio of exposure proportions; it is what you would compute in a cohort study, and the exam places it there to catch people who have not drawn the table.

Rule: Write the 2x2 table, then OR = (exposed cases x unexposed controls)/(unexposed cases x exposed controls).

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Childhood residence near a major road in 150 cases and 150 matched controls
A public health team identifies 150 adults with a lifetime history of agoraphobia and 150 matched controls without it, and asks each about living within 200 metres of a major road during childhood. The table shows the results: 30 of the cases and 12 of the controls report this exposure. Which of the following CANNOT be calculated from this study?
  1. The odds of exposure among cases
  2. The control exposure rate
  3. The relative risk of agoraphobia associated with the exposure
  4. The case exposure rate
  5. The odds ratio for exposure
Show the working
Answer: C The relative risk of agoraphobia associated with the exposure

Relative risk is the incidence of disease among the exposed divided by the incidence among the unexposed. To calculate it you need to follow exposed and unexposed people forward and count new cases, which is what a cohort study does. A case-control study recruits a fixed number of cases and controls, so the proportion with disease in any exposure group is an artefact of the recruitment ratio.

All of the exposure rates and odds in this study are valid because they are calculated within the case group or within the control group. The odds ratio is valid because it is unaffected by the case:control ratio. The relative risk is not.

When the disease is rare the odds ratio approximates the relative risk, and papers often describe it in relative risk language, but that is an approximation, not a calculation.

Rule: Case-control studies give odds ratios, never relative risks, because the proportion with disease is fixed by the investigator.
Trap: Assuming that a 2x2 table always yields a relative risk.
QuantityHow it would be calculatedAvailable here?
Odds of exposure among cases30/120Can be calculated
Case exposure rate30/150Can be calculated
Control exposure rate12/150Can be calculated
Odds ratio for exposure(30 x 138)/(12 x 120) = 2.9Can be calculated
Relative risk of agoraphobiaNeeds incidence in exposed and unexposed peopleCannot: the 150:150 ratio was chosen by the investigators
Everything calculated within a group, or as a ratio of odds, is valid; the relative risk needs a cohort.

Source: Kirkwood BR, Sterne JAC (2003). Essential Medical Statistics, 2nd ed. Blackwell.

Odds and probability describe the same information differently. The probability of high neuroticism among the depressed is 60/75 = 0.8; the odds are 60/15 = 4, because odds divide those with the feature by those without it rather than by the whole group. Odds and probability are related by odds = p/(1 minus p).

Among the 75 depressed respondents, 60 scored high and 15 low on neuroticism. Odds = 60/15 = 4. The question asks for odds, not an odds ratio, so the non-depressed row is not needed. If it had asked for the odds ratio, that would be (60 x 125)/(15 x 50) = 10.

Read the question twice: odds, odds ratio, probability and relative risk are all available from one table and the exam switches between them.

Rule: Odds within a group = number with the characteristic / number without it; an odds ratio compares two such odds.
Trap: Calculating the odds ratio when the question asks for the odds in one group.

A case-control study nested in a Welsh primary care database compares 2400 adults over 70 who sustained an injurious fall with 9600 matched controls. Odds ratios adjusted for age and sex are shown in the table. Which factor is the strongest predictor of an injurious fall in this analysis?
  1. Antidepressant prescription
  2. Diagnosis of Parkinson's disease
  3. Benzodiazepine prescription
  4. Alcohol above 14 units per week
  5. Current smoking
Show the working
Answer: C Benzodiazepine prescription

An odds ratio above 1 means the factor is associated with higher odds of the outcome; the further from 1, the stronger the association. The confidence interval shows precision: an interval that includes 1 means the association is not statistically significant at 5%, whatever the point estimate.

Scanning the table, benzodiazepine prescription has the largest odds ratio (2.35) and its interval 1.80 to 3.07 lies entirely above 1. Parkinson's disease (1.90) and antidepressants (1.62) are also significant but weaker. Smoking's interval includes 1 and is not significant.

Be careful when the largest point estimate has a wide interval that crosses 1: strength and significance are separate judgements, and a question can ask about either.

Rule: In a table of odds ratios, the strongest predictor has the odds ratio furthest from 1 with a confidence interval that excludes 1.
Trap: Choosing on familiarity of the risk factor rather than on the numbers in the table.
Ranked by point estimate: benzodiazepines (2.35, interval 1.80 to 3.07) sit furthest right and clear of 1; smoking (1.12) and BMI (0.95) cross 1.

Source: Petrie A, Sabin C (2019). Medical Statistics at a Glance, 4th ed. Wiley Blackwell.

  2. Current smoking is not significantly associated with injurious falls
  3. Benzodiazepines cause injurious falls
  4. A diagnosis of Parkinson's disease is significantly associated with injurious falls
  5. Vitamin D supplementation is associated with lower odds of an injurious fall
Show the working
Answer: C Benzodiazepines cause injurious falls

Odds ratios with confidence intervals tell you whether, and how strongly, a factor is associated with an outcome. They cannot tell you that the factor causes the outcome. People prescribed benzodiazepines may differ from others in anxiety, sleep disturbance, frailty or alcohol use, any of which could raise fall risk; adjustment for age and sex does not address these.

Each of the four association statements can be checked against the table: three intervals exclude 1 (benzodiazepines, Parkinson's disease, vitamin D) and one includes it (smoking). The causal claim about benzodiazepines is the one that goes beyond the data.

Exam stems that say cause, prevent or eliminate are usually the wrong conclusion to draw from observational tables, unless the question is explicitly about Bradford Hill criteria.

Rule: A case-control odds ratio measures association; causation needs more than a table of odds ratios.
Trap: Treating a large, significant odds ratio as proof of cause.
Three intervals clear 1 upwards, one clears it downwards and three cross it; none of them can say 'cause'.

Source: Rothman KJ (2012). Epidemiology: An Introduction, 2nd ed. Oxford University Press.

The absolute risk reduction is the simplest expression of benefit: the proportion of patients who have the bad outcome on control minus the proportion who have it on treatment. It is a difference, not a ratio, so it carries information about how common the outcome was to begin with, and it is the quantity that the number needed to treat is built from.

Define the event as non-recovery. The control event rate is 150 / 200 = 0.75 and the experimental event rate is 75 / 200 = 0.375. ARR = 0.75 minus 0.375 = 0.375, which is the same as the absolute benefit increase in recovery (0.625 minus 0.25).

The exam offers the two raw rates, the RRR and the RBI as distractors; write CER and EER down first and subtract.

Trap: Reporting one of the raw event rates instead of their difference.

  1. 0.25

  3. 0.50
  4. 0.75
  5. 1.5
Show the working
Answer: C 0.50

The relative risk reduction tells you what proportion of the baseline risk the treatment removes. It is the ARR divided by the control event rate, or equivalently 1 minus the relative risk. Because it is relative it looks the same whether the baseline risk is 75% or 0.75%, which is why it can exaggerate benefit for rare outcomes.

With CER = 0.75 and EER = 0.375 for non-recovery, ARR = 0.375 and RRR = 0.375 / 0.75 = 0.50. The relative risk is 0.375 / 0.75 = 0.5, and 1 minus 0.5 gives the same answer.

Marketing and the exam both prefer the RRR because it is the bigger number; always ask what the absolute difference was.

Rule: RRR = (CER minus EER) / CER, the ARR expressed as a fraction of the control risk.
Trap: Dividing by the experimental rate, or quoting the ARR as if it were relative.
StepWorkingResult
1CER (non-recovery, placebo) = 150 / 2000.75
2EER (non-recovery, SNRI) = 75 / 2000.375
3ARR = 0.75 minus 0.3750.375
4RRR = ARR / CER = 0.375 / 0.750.50 (keyed)
5Check: RR = 0.375 / 0.75 = 0.5; 1 minus 0.50.50
Working: RRR = 0.375 / 0.75 = 0.50

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Recovery at 12 weeks in a trial of a new SNRI in young adults with depression
Using the same trial table, what is the number needed to treat with the SNRI for one additional patient to recover?
  1. 2
  2. 3
  3. 4
  4. 5
  5. 8
Show the working
Answer: B 3

The number needed to treat converts an absolute difference into a number of patients: how many you must treat for one extra good outcome. It is the reciprocal of the ARR (or the ABI, which is the same number seen from the recovery side). It is always rounded up, because you cannot treat a fraction of a patient and rounding down would overstate the benefit.

ARR = 0.75 minus 0.375 = 0.375, so NNT = 1 / 0.375 = 2.67, which rounds up to 3. Treating three patients with the SNRI rather than placebo yields one additional recovery.

The exam keys the rounded-up value; if 2.67 and 3 were both offered, 3 is the conventional answer.

Rule: NNT = 1 / ARR, rounded up to the next whole patient.
Trap: Using 1 / RRR (which would give 2) or rounding down.
15 extra recoveries per 40 treated: 40 / 15 = 2.67, so 3 patients per extra recovery

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

The table shows 6-month remission in a trial comparing group CBT with supportive counselling for adolescent depression. Treating non-remission as the event, what is the absolute risk reduction with group CBT?

  2. 0.30
  3. 0.50
  4. 0.60

Show the working
Answer: B 0.30

Absolute risk reduction is the plain difference in the proportion of patients with the bad outcome between control and treatment. It depends on the baseline rate, which is its strength: it tells you how much benefit a typical patient actually gets.

Non-remission occurs in 100 / 200 = 0.50 of the counselling group and 40 / 200 = 0.20 of the CBT group. ARR = 0.50 minus 0.20 = 0.30. The same number appears as the absolute benefit increase in remission (0.80 minus 0.50).

Both raw rates are offered as distractors, as is the RRR. Write down CER and EER, then subtract.

Rule: ARR = CER minus EER, using the event you have defined as bad.
Trap: Quoting the control event rate as the ARR.
StepWorkingResult
1CER (non-remission on counselling) = 100 / 2000.50
2EER (non-remission on CBT) = 40 / 2000.20
3ARR = 0.50 minus 0.200.30 (keyed)
4Check from the remission side: 0.80 minus 0.500.30
Working: ARR = 0.50 minus 0.20 = 0.30

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Using the same adolescent depression trial table, what is the relative risk reduction in non-remission with group CBT compared with supportive counselling?

  2. 0.40
  3. 0.50
  4. 0.60

Show the working
Answer: D 0.60

The relative risk reduction expresses the ARR as a fraction of the control group's risk. It is also 1 minus the relative risk. Because it strips out the baseline rate it is portable across populations but can mislead about the absolute benefit.

CER for non-remission = 0.50, EER = 0.20. RR = 0.20 / 0.50 = 0.40, so RRR = 1 minus 0.40 = 0.60. Equivalently ARR / CER = 0.30 / 0.50 = 0.60. Group CBT removed 60% of the risk of non-remission.

The relative risk (0.40) and the relative benefit (1.6) are tempting near-misses; the reduction is 1 minus RR.

Rule: RRR = ARR / CER = 1 minus the relative risk.
Trap: Giving the relative risk itself rather than one minus it.
StepWorkingResult
1CER (non-remission, counselling) = 100 / 2000.50
2EER (non-remission, CBT) = 40 / 2000.20
3RR = 0.20 / 0.500.40
4RRR = 1 minus 0.400.60 (keyed)
5Check: ARR / CER = 0.30 / 0.500.60
Working: RRR = 1 minus 0.40 = 0.60

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Answer: C 4

The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the absolute risk reduction. It expresses the benefit as a count of patients: how many must receive the better treatment for one extra patient to have the good outcome. A low NNT means a large absolute benefit.

ARR = 0.50 minus 0.20 = 0.30, so NNT = 1 / 0.30 = 3.33. Rounding up gives 4: four adolescents treated with group CBT rather than counselling produce one additional remission at six months.

The rounded-down value (3) is the standard distractor; convention is to round up so that the benefit is not overstated.

Rule: NNT = 1 / ARR, always rounded up.
Trap: Rounding 3.33 down to 3.
3 extra remissions per 10 treated: 10 / 3 = 3.33, rounded up to 4

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Outcomes in a head-to-head trial of a new antipsychotic against an older comparator
The table shows the results of a trial comparing a new antipsychotic (drug Z) with an older active comparator in 800 patients with schizophrenia. What is the response rate in the control group?

  2. 0.30
  3. 0.50
  4. 0.70
  5. 0.75
Show the working
Answer: D 0.70

Every effect measure starts with two event rates: the proportion with the outcome in the control arm (CER) and in the experimental arm (EER). In an active-comparator trial the established drug is the control and the new drug is experimental, whatever order the table lists them in.

Control response rate = 280 / 400 = 0.70. This is the baseline against which drug Z's response will be judged.

Mis-identifying the control arm reverses the sign of every subsequent calculation, so settle it before you do anything else.

Rule: Event rate = events / number in that arm; identify which arm is the control first.
Trap: Treating the new drug as the control because it appears second in the table.
StepWorkingResult
1Identify the control armolder comparator, the established drug
2Responders in the control arm280 of 400
3Control response rate = 280 / 4000.70 (keyed)
Working: control response rate = 280 / 400 = 0.70

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

Answer: D 0.50

The experimental event rate is the second building block. Here the event of interest is improvement, a good outcome, so the rates are benefit rates rather than risk rates, but the arithmetic is the same.

Experimental response rate = 200 / 400 = 0.50. Drug Z therefore produced a lower response rate than the comparator (0.70), which will make its absolute benefit increase negative.

Keep both rates side by side (0.70 control, 0.50 experimental) before moving to differences and reciprocals.

Rule: EER = events in the experimental arm / number in the experimental arm.
Trap: Reading the EPSE column instead of the response column.
StepWorkingResult
1Identify the experimental armdrug Z, the new drug
2Responders on drug Z200 of 400
3Experimental response rate = 200 / 4000.50 (keyed)
4Compare with the control rate0.50 is below 0.70, so drug Z responds less
Working: experimental response rate = 200 / 400 = 0.50

Answer: C 0.30

A trial produces more than one event rate. Response rates feed the NNT; adverse event rates feed the number needed to harm. Both are simple proportions within each arm and must be kept apart.

Control EPSE rate = 120 / 400 = 0.30. Nearly a third of patients on the older comparator developed extrapyramidal side effects.

Distractors mix columns; read the column heading before dividing.

Rule: Adverse event rate = adverse events / number in the arm, calculated separately from the response rate.
Trap: Dividing EPSE by the number who improved rather than by the arm total.
StepWorkingResult
1Read the EPSE column for the control arm120 of 400
2Control EPSE rate = 120 / 4000.30 (keyed)
3Distractor check: 120 / 280 (responders)0.43, wrong denominator
Working: control EPSE rate = 120 / 400 = 0.30

Challenge 30 · 13.4 Measures of treatment impact · 3.2.12.2

  2. 0.05
  3. 0.10
  4. 0.25
  5. 0.30
Show the working
Answer: B 0.05

The experimental adverse event rate is the proportion of all patients in the experimental arm who experienced the harm. It will be compared with the control rate to produce the absolute harm difference.

Drug Z EPSE rate = 20 / 400 = 0.05. Drug Z therefore caused far fewer extrapyramidal effects than the comparator (0.30), even though it produced fewer responses.

The near-miss distractor (0.10) comes from dividing by the 200 responders; the denominator is always the full arm.

Rule: Divide by everyone in the arm, not by a subgroup.
Trap: Using responders as the denominator.
StepWorkingResult
1Read the EPSE column for drug Z20 of 400
2Drug Z EPSE rate = 20 / 4000.05 (keyed)
3Distractor check: 20 / 200 (responders)0.10, wrong denominator
Working: drug Z EPSE rate = 20 / 400 = 0.05

Source: Cook RJ, Sackett DL (1995). The number needed to treat: a clinically useful measure of treatment effect. BMJ, 310: 452-454.

C) 0.06

Remember. Absolute difference = EER minus CER; when it is harm it is an absolute risk increase.

Trap. Writing 6 when the scale is a proportion.

Why not the others.
A) 0.6: Decimal error: 6% is 0.06.
B) 1.2: 1.2 is the relative risk (0.36 / 0.30).

Remember. Read p-values time point by time point; means describe groups, not individuals.

B) Every patient on the programme wards improved: Group means cannot show that every individual improved.

Trap. Defining ICC as variation within clusters.

Why not the others.
A) Variation between the treatment arms: Treatment effect is what the trial estimates, not the ICC.
B) Variation among patients within the same ward: Within-ward variation is the remainder, not the ICC.
